crest-whitestrips.summary: Over-the-counter peroxide strips that lighten teeth by a shade or two over one to three weeks for a brighter smile.

quick.overview:
Crest Whitestrips are thin plastic strips coated with peroxide gel that you press onto your teeth to lift stain and brighten your smile. They launched in 2001 and are among the best-known at-home whitening products in the US.

The peroxide gel oxidises the pigment molecules that cause staining in and on the enamel, while the strip holds the gel against the tooth surface. Several randomized trials of the product have been published, and general reviews describe strip systems as lightening teeth by about one or two shades.
quick.how: Users stick the strips on for a set time each day over a course of one to three weeks. They are used on yellowing and surface stain from food, drinks, tobacco and ageing. Results vary with starting tooth colour and can fade over time.
quick.risks: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects. The strips are not designed for crowns, veneers or fillings. Regulators differ on peroxide strength: the EU limits retail products to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.

angle.text: Peroxide gel on the strip lifts stain from the tooth surface, so teeth look a shade or two lighter after a one-to-three-week course. The change in tooth colour is visible and measurable, and clinical trials have reported it.

custom-bleaching-trays.summary: Dentist-fitted trays that hold peroxide gel against every tooth for an even, whiter shade; the long-standing at-home alternative to strips.

quick.overview:
Custom bleaching trays are mouthpieces moulded to your teeth and filled with a peroxide gel, usually carbamide peroxide, to lighten tooth colour evenly across the whole smile. They are usually prescribed by a dentist and have been described in dental literature since the late 1960s, with a 1989 paper supporting the method.

The tray keeps the gel in contact with every tooth, where the peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in enamel and dentine. Tray bleaching is described as producing about one or two shades of lightening within days, with some fading afterwards. Published work found in the sources is limited to laboratory studies of how trays and gel strength affect stain.
quick.how: Trays are worn at home for a set period, ranging from a few hours daily to overnight, under dentist supervision. Carbamide peroxide is commonly used because its effects were reported to last longer than hydrogen peroxide.
quick.risks: Sensitivity is the most common side effect. Gum irritation or burns are linked to high peroxide concentrations and ill-fitting trays. EU rules allow up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide only under dental supervision.

angle.text: A tray moulded to your teeth holds peroxide gel against every surface, so the shade lightens evenly and your smile looks whiter. It is a long-standing alternative to strips, and the change in tooth colour is visible.

whitening-mouth-rinse.summary: Peroxide mouthwash used as a low-effort way to gradually lighten tooth stain and brighten your smile over weeks.

quick.overview:
Whitening rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes containing a peroxide, used to lighten tooth colour and reduce surface stain with very little effort.

The peroxide oxidises stain molecules on the teeth, though contact time is short compared with strips or trays, so results are described as gradual. Published work on rinses is mostly laboratory studies, case reports and product analyses rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.
quick.how: Users swish the rinse as part of the daily routine, twice daily for about a minute each time in the usual description. Visible results can take up to three months.
quick.risks: One case report documents a chemical gum burn after misuse. Peroxide at 10 percent or more is described as able to burn tissue, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.

angle.text: A peroxide rinse contacts the teeth twice a day and gradually lifts surface stain, giving a slightly brighter smile over weeks to a few months. It is the lowest-effort whitening option; supporting research is mainly laboratory work.

potassium-nitrate-desensitising-toothpas.summary: Desensitising toothpaste that whitening users reach for to calm sensitivity so they can finish a bleaching course; studied for dentine pain generally.

quick.overview:
This is a toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, made to reduce dentine hypersensitivity, the sharp pain from exposed dentine in response to cold, heat or touch. Whitening users use it because tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect of peroxide bleaching.

It helps whitening indirectly: calmer teeth make it easier to complete a course and reach a brighter smile. Cochrane reviews have assessed potassium toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity, and laboratory work has examined whether potassium nitrate blocks dentinal tubules. Trials aimed specifically at whitening sensitivity were not found.
quick.how: Used as an ordinary toothpaste around peroxide bleaching. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article says potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride toothpastes can ease whitening sensitivity.
quick.risks: It is an over-the-counter product with no specific risks noted in the sources. There is no evidence it permanently prevents whitening sensitivity, so it eases rather than eliminates it.

angle.text: Calming dentine sensitivity makes it easier to keep up a peroxide whitening course, which leads to a whiter smile at the end. It has been studied for dentine pain in general, not for whitening outcomes specifically.

prophy-paste-polish.summary: The gritty polishing paste hygienists use to lift surface stain during a cleaning, leaving teeth cleaner, smoother and brighter-looking.

quick.overview:
Prophy paste is an abrasive polishing paste applied by a dental professional with a rotating rubber cup during a cleaning. It removes surface stain and plaque, leaving teeth looking cleaner and smoother.

Fine abrasive particles in the paste are spun against the tooth to polish the surface and lift deposits. It works on external stain rather than the tooth's inner colour. Available research is mostly laboratory work on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces; no cosmetic trial of stain removal was found.
quick.how: It is part of a professional dental cleaning appointment, applied by a hygienist or dentist.
quick.risks: Lab studies show polishing pastes can change the roughness and gloss of composite resin restorations. It is a professional procedure.

angle.text: A gritty paste polishes the enamel and lifts surface stain, so teeth look cleaner and brighter right after a cleaning. Research on it focuses on abrasivity and dental materials rather than cosmetic results.

lip-suction-pump.summary: A vacuum cup that temporarily swells the lips so they look fuller within minutes.

quick.overview:
A lip suction pump is a hand-held vacuum device placed over the lips to make them look fuller. The swelling is visible within minutes and is temporary.

Wikipedia's lip plumper article describes the vacuum as raising blood pressure in the lips, causing temporary swelling. It is one of several non-injection plumping approaches, alongside topical plumpers whose irritant ingredients such as capsaicin cause swelling. Published information on the devices is sparse and no studies of them were found.
quick.how: Users place the cup over the lips for a short session before going out or taking photos. The fuller look fades after use.
quick.risks: No risks specific to the device are documented in the sources found. The effect is temporary swelling.

angle.text: A vacuum cup over the lips draws blood to them, causing temporary swelling that makes them look fuller within minutes. The effect fades afterward, and no studies of these devices were found.

earwell-infant-ear-molding.summary: A non-surgical splint that reshapes a newborn's soft ear cartilage in the first weeks of life, correcting lop or prominent ears without surgery.

quick.overview:
EarWell is a non-surgical molding system placed on a newborn's ear to reshape congenital differences such as constricted (lop) ears, Stahl's ear and prominent ears, so the ear holds a typical shape and position. It is a pediatric medical device and an alternative to later ear surgery (otoplasty).

Researchers describe newborn ear cartilage as unusually pliable in the first weeks of life, attributed to circulating maternal estrogens. A splint holds the ear in a corrected shape during this window so the cartilage sets in the new form. Published series from several centers, including in China and the United States, report that most treated ears improve when treatment starts early; no randomized controlled trial appears among the studies reviewed.
quick.how: A shaped device is adhered to the infant's ear for a period of weeks, started as early as possible after birth. Decisions are made with a pediatric or plastic-surgery clinician.
quick.risks: Studies describe treatment as non-invasive, with outcomes depending strongly on how early it begins and on deformity severity. Skin irritation from adhesives is a general consideration for any taped device.

angle.text: A splint worn in the first weeks of life reshapes soft newborn ear cartilage so lop or prominent ears set in a typical form without surgery. Clinical series report good results when treatment starts early.

dermastamp-0-5mm.summary: A handheld needle stamp used for microneedling; forum users apply it to brows and skin for texture and to help topicals absorb.

quick.overview:
A dermastamp is a small handheld microneedling tool whose short needle head is pressed straight down onto the skin, unlike a rolling dermaroller. On looksmax.org it is discussed for fuller brows alongside minoxidil, for lines around the eyes and for skin texture, with 0.5 mm a commonly discussed needle length.

Microneedling punctures the skin repeatedly with tiny needles, creating micro-channels. Wikipedia describes it as a cosmetic procedure used for scarring and acne and notes a pilot study of combining it with minoxidil for hair loss. Forum users also say it helps topicals absorb. Published work found on stamps themselves is laboratory-style research on microneedle-assisted drug delivery.
quick.how: Users press the stamp onto the skin or brow area, often before applying a topical, and compare it with rollers in forum threads. Frequency is a common forum question.
quick.risks: Non-sterile or poorly handled needling carries infection risk. Wikipedia reports a 2024 CDC report of three HIV diagnoses among patients of one New Mexico spa offering microneedling with platelet-rich plasma, attributed to infection-control concerns in non-medical settings.

angle.text: Users press the stamp onto skin and brows to make micro-channels that they say help topicals absorb and soften fine lines. Microneedling has been studied for scars and acne; the brow and under-eye uses come from forum reports.

red-light-mask-omnilux-currentbody.summary: Consumer LED face masks worn at home for smoother, clearer skin and fewer wrinkles; red-light therapy has mixed, often preliminary results.

quick.overview:
Red light masks are wearable LED devices that illuminate the face with red, sometimes near-infrared or blue, light. Brands such as Omnilux and CurrentBody sell them for home use, aimed at wrinkles, acne, puffiness and general skin quality.

The technique is LED light therapy or photobiomodulation. Descriptions say red and near-infrared light penetrate skin and act mainly on mitochondria, particularly cytochrome c oxidase, which proponents link to more collagen production and less inflammation. Dermatology research on the approach has had mixed and often preliminary results, and no trial of a specific Omnilux or CurrentBody mask was located.
quick.how: Users wear the mask over the face for regular sessions as part of a skincare routine, and results are generally described as gradual.
quick.risks: LED therapy is described as having fewer side effects than lasers. Reported effects for low-level light include itching, red spots and mild allergic reactions, usually temporary.

angle.text: Red light reaches skin cells and is proposed to raise collagen and repair signalling, which users hope leads to fewer wrinkles and clearer skin. Red-light therapy has been studied for skin ageing and acne with mixed results, and consumer masks are less studied than clinical devices.

photorejuvenation-led-panel.summary: Home red and near-infrared LED panel aimed at the face or body for fine lines, skin texture, acne and hair growth.

quick.overview:
A photorejuvenation LED panel is a flat array of LEDs, usually red and near-infrared, that users hold or mount near the face or body at home. It is associated with smoother skin, fewer fine lines, clearer skin and hair growth.

The underlying technique is photobiomodulation: low-level light absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria, thought to raise ATP production and nitric oxide release, a pathway described as suggested rather than settled. Red and near-infrared wavelengths (roughly 600 to 1000 nm) reach deeper into tissue than blue or green light. Summaries report studies of red-light LED therapy for collagen enhancement, acne, rosacea and hair loss, without comparing home panels to clinical equipment.
quick.how: Users aim the panel at the face or body for regular sessions over weeks, typically as an add-on to a skincare routine.
quick.risks: Photobiomodulation is generally described as safe, with infrequent transient itching, red spots or mild allergic reactions. Regulatory status of consumer panels was not established in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Red and near-infrared light is absorbed by skin cells, with the proposed result of more cell repair and collagen activity for smoother skin and possibly hair growth. The mechanism comes from lab and clinical-device studies; trials of consumer panels are limited.

ultrasound-scaler-home.summary: Consumer version of the dental ultrasonic scaler that users run over teeth to remove visible tartar and stain between dental visits.

quick.overview:
A home ultrasonic scaler is a consumer tool modelled on the instrument dental hygienists use to remove tartar, plaque and stain, so teeth look cleaner and brighter. Appearance communities discuss it for clearing visible tartar between dental visits.

Professional scalers vibrate at high frequency to loosen deposits and use a liquid spray to cool the tip and flush debris. Published research covers professional devices, and no studies of home-use scalers were found.
quick.how: Users work the tool over the tooth surfaces at home between professional cleanings.
quick.risks: Professional-setting research reports aerosol and splatter generation and notes possible damage to enamel, restorations and root surfaces. Home-use safety data were not found.

angle.text: Vibration breaks up tartar and lifts stain, leaving teeth looking cleaner and brighter. Research covers professional ultrasonic scalers; home units have not been studied the same way.

1-testosterone-1-test-dihydroboldenone.summary: A DHT-derived designer steroid once sold online as a muscle-building supplement; controlled in the US since 2005 and untested in human trials.

quick.overview:
1-Testosterone (1-Test, dihydroboldenone) is a synthetic androgen, the 5-alpha-reduced derivative of boldenone. It was sold online as a prohormone supplement for bodybuilders seeking muscle size and a fuller physique.

It binds the androgen receptor selectively, which is the route to faster muscle protein gain. An animal study reported potency comparable to testosterone propionate in androgen-sensitive tissues. Only animal data and doping-detection literature were found; no clinical trials in people.
quick.how: It was sold as a supplement or prohormone in the past. It became a US controlled substance in 2005, ending legal online sales.
quick.risks: In the animal study it also increased liver weight. It has been a US Schedule III controlled substance since 2005, and human safety has not been studied.

angle.text: It activates the androgen receptor, which is the route to faster muscle protein gain and a bigger, fuller physique. It was sold online as a supplement until 2005 and has been a US controlled substance since; there are no human trials of its effects.

methyl-1-testosterone-m1t.summary: An oral designer androgen once sold in supplements for muscle size; known from animal work and a kidney-injury case report.

quick.overview:
Methyl-1-testosterone (M1T) is an orally active synthetic androgen, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of 1-testosterone. It appeared in early-2000s over-the-counter supplements aimed at bodybuilders chasing muscle growth and a bigger physique. It was never marketed for medical use.

It is an androgen receptor agonist, and a 2011 study identified it in a supplement and tested receptor affinity and anabolic and androgenic potency in animal and in vitro models. Research is limited to that animal and in vitro work, analytical papers and a case report.
quick.how: It was sold in supplements in the 2000s without medical approval; it is oral.
quick.risks: A case report describes acute kidney injury after combining it with ciclosporin. It is on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: It activates the androgen receptor, the route to more muscle growth and a bigger physique, and it was sold in early-2000s supplements for that purpose. Published material is animal work and a kidney-injury case report; the muscle-building use is anecdotal.

methylstenbolone-m-sten-hybrid.summary: An oral designer androgen sold online as a supplement or research chemical for muscle gain; published human material is a case report of liver injury.

quick.overview:
Methylstenbolone (M-Sten, Methyl-Sten, Ultradrol) is a synthetic oral androgen, the 17-alpha-methylated derivative of stenbolone. Lifters use it seeking muscle gain and a harder physique. It was never introduced for medical use.

It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist, and 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity. Published work is mainly metabolism and doping-detection studies, supplement analyses and a case report; it has not been trialled in people.
quick.how: It has been sold online as a nutritional supplement or research chemical in oral form.
quick.risks: A case report links a product containing it to cholestatic jaundice. It is prohibited in sport and has no approved medical use.

angle.text: It activates the androgen receptor, the route to faster muscle protein gain and a harder-looking physique, and lifters use it for that. It has never been trialled in people; the published human material is a case report of cholestatic jaundice.

methyldienolone-methyldienolone-m-dien.summary: An unmarketed oral 19-nor androgen discussed in bodybuilding circles for muscle; almost nothing is published beyond detection chemistry.

quick.overview:
Methyldienolone (RU-3467) is an oral 17-alpha-methylated 19-nortestosterone derivative that appears in bodybuilding discussion as a muscle-building compound. It was never marketed as a drug.

It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist, which is the proposed route to anabolic muscle effects. The literature consists of chemistry and doping-control papers, and no pharmacokinetic detail or human data were found.
quick.how: It has no marketed form; it is discussed in bodybuilding communities as an oral compound.
quick.risks: No adverse-effect data were found. It is prohibited in sport and listed as a US Schedule III substance per Wikipedia.

angle.text: Bodybuilding discussion treats it as an oral androgen that activates the androgen receptor for more muscle mass. Almost nothing is published beyond detection chemistry, and its muscle effect in people has not been studied.

dimethyltrienolone-dimethyltren-ru-2420.summary: A never-marketed trenbolone analog reported in animal assays at far above methyltestosterone potency; no human data exist.

quick.overview:
Dimethyltrienolone (RU-2420) is an experimental oral anabolic steroid first described in 1967 by Roussel Uclaf and never sold as a medicine. It comes up in bodybuilding circles for its reported potency, aimed at more muscle mass.

It activates the androgen and progesterone receptors strongly and, like trenbolone, is not converted by aromatase or 5-alpha-reductase; methyl groups at two positions resist liver breakdown, allowing oral activity. Animal bioassays reported more than 100 times the potency of methyltestosterone, and Wikipedia attributes the description 'perhaps the most potent' to a secondary source. All of this rests on rodent and receptor-binding work.
quick.how: It circulates only as an unregulated research chemical taken orally; it has no approved form.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. Reference sources describe it as expected to be highly liver-toxic, inferred from related compounds, and note progestogenic effects. It has no approved medical use.

angle.text: A never-marketed trenbolone analog that binds the androgen receptor very strongly in animal assays, which is why it comes up for muscle gain. No human studies exist, so its effect on physique is based on rodent and receptor work.

metribolone-r1881-methyltrienolone.summary: A lab-standard androgen receptor ligand dropped as a drug for liver toxicity; it also turns up in doping cases and bodybuilding circles.

quick.overview:
Metribolone (R1881, methyltrienolone) is an oral anabolic steroid, the 17-alpha-methyl derivative of trenbolone, made in the 1960s. It was tried for advanced breast cancer but dropped because of liver toxicity at very low doses. Since the mid-1970s it has been a standard laboratory reagent.

It binds the androgen receptor very tightly and resists breakdown by 5-alpha-reductase and aromatase, which is why radiolabelled R1881 is used to measure receptor binding and why it appears in bodybuilding talk for muscle mass. In rats it was reported at 120 to 300 times the oral anabolic potency of methyltestosterone, though Wikipedia notes comparable potency has not been seen in humans.
quick.how: Outside the lab it has appeared in sports doping and underground bodybuilding use; it has no approved form.
quick.risks: Documented effects include liver toxicity and virilisation. It is banned in sport, has no approved use, and has no controlled modern human studies.

angle.text: It binds the androgen receptor extremely tightly, which is why it is a lab standard and why it surfaces in underground muscle-building talk. Its physique use rests on anecdote; clinical development ended over liver toxicity.

tetrahydrogestrinone-thg-the-clear.summary: The 2003 designer steroid built to slip past doping tests, taken by athletes for muscle and performance; never studied in people.

quick.overview:
THG, nicknamed The Clear, is an oral steroid made by modifying the gynecological drug gestrinone, taken by athletes for muscle and performance. It surfaced in 2003 when a used syringe was handed to anti-doping officials, and Don Catlin's UCLA laboratory identified it; it became central to the BALCO scandal.

It binds the androgen receptor about as tightly as DHT, also activates progesterone receptors, and binds the glucocorticoid receptor. Rat studies showed it promotes muscle growth. It is known mostly from doping history and detection research rather than from appearance or bodybuilding use.
quick.how: It was used by athletes as an oral steroid designed to evade existing doping tests; it was never approved for medical use.
quick.risks: It has never been tested in clinical trials, so effects in people are uncharacterised; infertility, acne and hirsutism are listed with prolonged use. It is a US Schedule III substance and banned in sport.

angle.text: A designer steroid made in 2003 to dodge doping tests, taken by athletes for more muscle mass. It is potent in laboratory assays and promoted muscle growth in rats, but has never been studied in people.

desoxymethyltestosterone-dmt-madol.summary: A 1960s oral steroid revived in 2005 as a designer doping agent and supplement ingredient for muscle gain; animal data only.

quick.overview:
Desoxymethyltestosterone (DMT, Madol) is an oral steroid, a 17-alpha-methyl derivative of DHT, invented by Max Huffman in 1961 and described in 1963 but never marketed. It re-emerged in 2005 when chemist Patrick Arnold produced it and supplied it to BALCO; it was later found in bodybuilding supplements sold for muscle gain and a harder look.

It activates the androgen receptor in vitro and increased muscle mass in castrated rats with little effect on prostate weight. All evidence comes from rat and cell studies; there are no clinical trials.
quick.how: It has been sold in over-the-counter supplements under names such as Pheraplex. Supplements labelled with it have sometimes contained other compounds.
quick.risks: Animal studies at higher doses reported liver damage and heart enlargement. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, Class C in the UK, and prohibited in sport.

angle.text: A modified form of DHT that activates the androgen receptor, sold in supplements for muscle gain and a harder look. Evidence is limited to rat and cell studies, with no human trials of the physique use.

prostanozol.summary: A designer prohormone steroid once sold in bodybuilding supplements for a stanozolol-like lean-muscle effect; now a US Schedule III substance.

quick.overview:
Prostanozol is a designer oral steroid sold in bodybuilding supplements from around 2005, aimed at a stanozolol-like effect of lean muscle and a drier look. It is a prodrug of a stanozolol analogue that lacks the 17-alpha-methyl group.

In the body it is described as converting to that analogue, which acts as an androgen receptor agonist. It has no clinical trials; published work covers doping-detection metabolism, supplement-contamination surveys and legal classification.
quick.how: It was sold as an oral dietary-supplement ingredient. In 2012 the US DEA classified it, with methasterone, as a Schedule III anabolic steroid.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been studied. It is a US Schedule III substance and prohibited in sport; a 2007 marathon runner received a two-year ban after testing positive for it and testosterone.

angle.text: A designer prohormone sold in supplements that converts in the body to a stanozolol-like steroid acting on the androgen receptor, for lean muscle and a drier look. It is now Schedule III in the US and has no clinical data.
